title: Identity Management Guide: SSO, MFA, Lifecycle, and Access Reviews
description: A practical identity management guide covering authentication, authorization, provisioning, least privilege, access reviews, recovery, and rollout risks.
author: PilotStack Editorial Team

sections.title: Separate Authentication From Authorization
sections.body: Authentication establishes who or what is requesting access; authorization determines what that identity may do. A platform can provide single sign-on without automatically solving application permissions, account lifecycle, or privileged access. Map the applications, user groups, service identities, and sensitive actions that need protection. Identify which system is authoritative for each identity attribute and how applications receive roles or groups. This prevents the selection process from treating one login screen as a complete identity architecture.

sections.title: Choose SSO and MFA Requirements
sections.body: List the applications that must support single sign-on, the identity protocols they use, and the user groups that require access. Decide where multi-factor authentication is mandatory, whether phishing-resistant methods are needed for privileged roles, and how exceptions are approved. Test recovery when a device is lost and how access is handled during an identity-provider outage. Verify plan limitations and supported protocols in current vendor documentation; do not assume that every connector, policy, or advanced control is included in every tier.

sections.title: Automate Joiner, Mover, and Leaver Events
sections.body: Identity lifecycle controls should match how people join, change roles, and leave the organization.
items: New accounts are created only after an authoritative approval or HR event.
Role changes update groups and application permissions without relying on manual reminders.
Departing users lose access promptly, including sessions, tokens, and connected applications.
Temporary workers and guests have an owner and an expiry or review date.
Service accounts have a named owner, purpose, and rotation or renewal plan.
Exceptions are logged and reviewed rather than becoming permanent shortcuts.

sections.title: Apply Least Privilege and Review Access
sections.body: Start with the minimum permissions needed for each role and elevate access only when justified. Separate administrative roles from ordinary daily accounts, limit standing privileges where feasible, and require additional review for sensitive actions. Build access reviews around real application ownership and data sensitivity. Review results should lead to a clear keep, change, or remove decision. A list of accounts is not enough if reviewers cannot tell what each account can access or why the access remains necessary.

sections.title: Plan Recovery and Resilience
sections.body: Identity systems are critical dependencies, so document how users and administrators recover from lost factors, locked accounts, provider outages, and compromised credentials. Protect emergency access accounts with strong controls, monitoring, and periodic tests. Verify backup administrator coverage and the process for rotating credentials after an incident. Avoid recovery methods that bypass the security level of the normal login without compensating controls. Test the recovery process with the people who will actually use it.

sections.title: Evaluate Logs, Integrations, and Governance
sections.body: Confirm that logs capture authentication events, administrative changes, policy decisions, and provisioning failures at a useful level of detail. Determine how long logs are retained and how they can be exported to the monitoring system. Inventory integrations and their permissions, and review how tokens are issued and revoked. Document identity data flows, retention, and vendor responsibilities. For regulated or sensitive environments, involve security and privacy stakeholders in the assessment and keep evidence of the decision.

sections.title: Pilot and Roll Out in Stages
sections.body: Choose a small group of applications and users that represents the real environment. Test normal sign-in, MFA enforcement, group changes, deprovisioning, guest access, and recovery. Define success criteria such as fewer manual access changes, faster offboarding, and fewer unresolved access exceptions. Roll out by application or group, monitor failed logins and support requests, and keep a rollback plan. Expand only after the team can operate the policies and troubleshoot common failures.
